text: A neural network almost never looks at one example on its own. It is handed a whole stack of examples at once, and the stack is stored in an array that can have any number of axes, which deep learning calls a tensor. A single number has no axes, a vector has one, a matrix has two, and a pile of matrices has three. Most bugs in model code are not deep mathematical errors but mismatched axes, so reading shapes fluently is worth real practice.

The shape of a tensor is the list of its axis lengths, read from the outside in. Think of a library: the first number counts the floors, the second counts the shelves on each floor, and the last counts the books on each shelf. A batch of sentences in a language model might have the shape thirty-two by one hundred and twenty-eight by seven hundred and sixty-eight, which reads as thirty-two sentences, each of one hundred and twenty-eight tokens, each token a vector of seven hundred and sixty-eight numbers.

Batching means stacking examples along a new first axis. If each example is a row of features, a batch is a matrix with one row per example. The payoff is that a single matrix multiplication now processes the whole batch: a batch of shape B by d in, times a weight matrix of shape d in by d out, gives B by d out. The inner lengths must match, because each output is a dot product of a row with a column, and they disappear, while the outer lengths survive.

Next we add a bias, but the bias has shape d out while the batch has shape B by d out. NumPy resolves this with broadcasting. It lines the two shapes up from the right and compares them axis by axis: two lengths are compatible if they are equal, or if one of them is one, or if one shape has run out of axes. A compatible short axis is stretched, without copying, to match the long one, so the same bias is added to every row, which is exactly what we meant.

The same rule can fail silently. Suppose the model's predictions have shape B by one, a column, and the targets have shape B, a flat vector. Subtracting them should give B errors, but broadcasting stretches the column across and the vector down, and produces a full B by B grid of every prediction minus every target. No error is raised, the loss is simply wrong, and the model trains on nonsense. Whenever a result is suspiciously large, print its shape.

Reductions remove axes. Summing a batch over axis zero collapses the examples and leaves one total per feature, while summing over the last axis collapses the features and leaves one total per example. Keeping a collapsed axis with length one, using keepdims, lets the result broadcast cleanly back against the original, which is how you normalise each row by its own sum.

Batches exist because hardware loves them: a graphics card multiplies one large matrix far faster than many small ones, and averaging the gradient over a batch gives a steadier step, as you saw with mini-batch gradient descent. When a language model trains, a batch of token ids of shape B by T passes through the embedding table and becomes B by T by d, and every layer after that preserves that shape. Next, we put batches to work in the training loop.
